rewrite.description: Lindsey Jordan's third Snail Mail album follows Valentine with clear-eyed, jangling guitar-pop, keeping the conversational, unadorned vocal delivery that made Lush a breakout. Harmonized guitars and a breezy, hushed touch carry songs about heartbreak, for listeners who want confessional indie rock without much studio gloss.
rewrite.lineage: Continues Snail Mail's own lineage from Lush through Valentine, staying within confessional, guitar-led jangle-pop songwriting.

rewrite.description: Sadie Dupuis's band follows Foil Deer by sharpening its knotty, dissonant guitar interplay into more outright pop structures. The hooks are bigger and the tempos brisker, but the lyrics stay confrontational about power and consent, for fans who like their guitar-pop with feedback and bite.

Speedy Ortiz's fourth album pushes the band's gnarled guitar interplay toward a vast, heavier sound, with long solos and walls of feedback. Sadie Dupuis's lyrics confront trauma and music-industry hypocrisy, making it the band's most expansive and pointed record.

Swearin's reunion album, its first for Merge, keeps the fuzzed, bittersweet guitar-pop of its Salinas Records releases while sounding fuller and more confident, with Allison Crutchfield and Kyle Gilbride trading songwriting duties as before. Harmonized guitars swing between bright jangle and noisy feedback, for fans of heart-on-sleeve Philadelphia DIY rock.
rewrite.lineage: A return, after a mid-2010s hiatus, to Swearin's own Philadelphia DIY guitar-pop lineage, a scene it shares with Waxahatchee, the project of Allison Crutchfield's twin sister Katie.

rewrite.description: Remember Sports' second album and first for Father/Daughter tightens the basement pop-punk of their Kenyon College beginnings into brisk, hook-first songs. Carmen Perry's elastic voice leads scrappy, fast guitar-pop that suits fans of loose, energetic DIY indie rock.
rewrite.lineage: The scrappy basement pop-punk starting point of Remember Sports' own arc, which grows toward the more collaborative, fuller songwriting of Slow Buzz and Like a Stone.

rewrite.description: Remember Sports' third Father/Daughter album builds on Slow Buzz's expanded arrangements, with the four members trading instruments and adding synths and drum machines to the guitar-pop core. Carmen Perry sings her sharpest lyrics yet about self-forgiveness, for listeners who like power pop with rough edges.

Warehouse's self-released debut is a kinetic, interlocking-guitar record fronted by Elaine Edenfield's commanding, sing-shouted vocals. It sits closer to Sonic Youth's angularity than to straightforward jangle-pop, but is still built on tightly wound guitar jams, for fans of wiry post-punk.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to Sonic Youth's interlocking-guitar vocabulary, part of the Atlanta post-punk/jangle underground.

rewrite.description: Warehouse's second album is a more concise, confident follow-up to Tesseract, keeping the interlocking guitar jams and Elaine Edenfield's fiery frontperson presence. The songs are leaner and more tightly wound, suiting listeners who like angular post-punk with a jangling edge.

Twin Peaks' Cadien Lake James steps out solo here, trading his main band's raw garage-pop for glimmering, tastefully electronic jangle-pop. It is a more polished, atmospheric record than his band's work, for listeners who like breezy guitar-pop with soft synth shading.

The Upper Peninsula band's self-titled album crams dense, hooky songs into a very short runtime, sounding indebted to Fountains of Wayne, PUP and Rozwell Kid in equal measure. It is power pop with a Midwestern punk snap, over almost before it starts.

Rui Gabriel's solo debut uses a light palette of fun grooves and Summerteeth-grade hooks to write self-aware songs about class and miscommunication. It is bright, sing-along power pop for listeners who like wry lyrics over tuneful, loose-limbed studio pop.
rewrite.lineage: A solo power-pop outlet that sounds indebted to Wilco's Summerteeth-era studio pop.

rewrite.description: Released under the band's earlier name Sioux Falls, this debut LP lays out the emo-tinged, twangy indie rock that would carry into Strange Ranger's later records. Quiet, hushed verses give way to sudden bursts of noise, for fans of sprawling emo-leaning guitar rock.
rewrite.lineage: The starting point of what became Strange Ranger's emo-twang crossover songwriting; it sounds akin to the Tiny Engines-adjacent DIY scene of bands like Free Cake for Every Creature.

rewrite.description: Strange Ranger's second album leans into a rawer, more spacious sound than their debut. It still balances hushed indie-folk passages against noisier emo-indebted guitar surges, suiting listeners who like quiet-loud dynamics with a twang.

The last Strange Ranger album before their turn toward electronic production, capping the band's emo-tinged indie rock era. Its arrangements are fuller and more anthemic than Rot Forever or Daymoon, for listeners who like big, yearning guitar rock.

rewrite.description: Strange Ranger return to guitar-based songwriting after an electronic detour, with a warmer, more settled sound. It closes out the emo-twang arc that began as Sioux Falls, for longtime fans and newcomers who like reflective, gently twangy indie rock.

Elise Okusami's second Oceanator album pairs big, emo-scaled guitar hooks with disarmingly direct lyrics about anxiety and dread. The songs move between crunchy pop-punk and more open, twangy indie-rock passages, for fans of cathartic, hook-heavy guitar music.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds descended from 2000s emo and pop-punk filtered through 2020s indie-rock production, close in spirit to the emo-twang crossover of bands like Strange Ranger.

rewrite.description: This home-recorded set mixes shoegaze walls of guitar with Primal Scream-style melodic touches and loose, woozy energy. It sits at the loud, twangy edge of countrygaze rather than its center, for listeners who like their noise-pop hazy and homespun.

rewrite.description: Sam Owens's fourth album as Sam Evian chases a warm, early-1970s Laurel Canyon feel across loose, groove-driven songs. Soft vocals, relaxed tempos and a live-band warmth make it for listeners who like cosmic-country-tinged soft rock.
rewrite.lineage: A Catskills singer-songwriter whose sound is indebted to the Laurel Canyon and Gram Parsons-adjacent cosmic-country lineage.

rewrite.description: A ten-song record where big hooks and feedback crash into banjo, mandolin, accordion and toy instruments, with shouted, harmonized vocals and loose studio chatter left in. It swings hard between hushed folk moments and punk blowouts, which puts it on the emo-twang side of the map. For listeners who like their folk-punk messy and their emo with a string band in the room.
rewrite.lineage: Folk-punk-leaning emo that sounds indebted to Titus Andronicus's rowdier moments and the Pinegrove-era emo-twang crossover; its acoustic instruments tie it to the DIY folk revival around the Core.
